title: When the captain calls
hookLine: ashore on a voyage you may gather shells, but when the captain calls, run to the ship (Enchiridion 7)

lines: AN ISLAND, A SPRING, A BEACH.
cards: A ship drops anchor off a rocky island. Fresh water is low, so the crew rows a few passengers ashore with jars to fill at a spring. The beach is lovely.
Shells glint in the shallows, wild onions grow in the dunes. Someone kneels to dig one up. Someone else wanders down the shore after a bigger shell.
Out on the water, the captain is watching the wind turn. Any minute now, a shout will come across the bay. Epictetus tells this little story in section seven of the handbook.

teach.h: ASHORE: SHELLS AND BULBS ARE FINE.
teach.b: On a voyage, Epictetus says, when the ship is at anchor and you go ashore for water, you may pick up a shellfish or a little bulb along the way. Nothing wrong with that.
But keep your mind on the ship, and keep turning around to listen for the captain. If he calls, drop everything and run, or you'll be hauled aboard tied up like the sheep. Then the turn.
So it is in life, he says.

teach.h: IN LIFE: A SPOUSE, A CHILD.
teach.b: If instead of a bulb and a shell you're given a spouse and a child, nothing stops you having them. But if the captain calls, run to the ship and leave them, without looking back.
And if you're old, don't wander far from the ship at all, or you may not make it when you're called.
What is the call? The handbook doesn't spell it out. Some readers hear the captain as God or the order of nature, and the call as death.
Others hear any moment that asks you to let go. It's a stark picture, and some readers find the family line hard to hear. Others notice what it allows: you may gather.
Love, collecting, beauty on the beach. The Stoic only asks that you keep one ear on the water.
The Greek for the captain is kybernetes, the one who steers. Dictionaries trace English govern back to it, through Latin gubernare. Someone else is steering the ship.
Your job ashore is simpler: enjoy the beach, fill your jar, listen.

how: Some Stoic practitioners enjoy small pleasures while keeping in mind that they may be called away from them, and practice setting them down easily.

the ship's captain, the one who steers

games.q: you're ashore with a jar, digging up a wild onion. the captain shouts from the ship. what does Epictetus say to do?
o: drop it all and run to the ship.
shout back for five more minutes.
games.why: throw it all away and run, he says, or you'll be thrown on board tied up like the sheep.

practice: Picture one pleasure waiting in your day, a coffee, a show, a long lunch, an afternoon with someone you like, and enjoy it there in your mind.
Then hear the shout across the water, the moment it's time to stop, and see yourself setting it down easily, the way you'd drop a shell back in the sand. Breathe, with one ear turned toward the ship.

wordCard.voice: Kybernetes, the Greek for the ship's captain: gather shells and bulbs ashore if you like, but keep listening, and when the call comes, go. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 7: the ship's captain, the steersman.

carryVoice: Your line: listen for the call. The beach is yours to enjoy, with one ear on the water. See you tomorrow.
